en: The Sūtra on Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra Spoken by the Buddha, with the Record of the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Mount Kukkuṭapada in the kingdom of Mathurā, together with a great assembly.
There were five hundred bhikṣus accompanying the Buddha.

At that time, the venerable Pūrṇa rose from his meditative seclusion in the late afternoon and went to where the Buddha was. He bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!”
“Please expound for me the essential Dharma; I shall practice it so that my body may enjoy boundless peace and security throughout the long night.
The Buddha said, “Listen attentively and reflect upon it well.”
Pūrṇa replied,
“So be it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Pūrṇa:

"With one's own eyes, they see beautiful forms that are pleasing to the eye, which they find delightful and crave; with their ears, they crave pleasant sounds; the nose perceives fragrant scents; the tongue knows delicious flavors; and the body contacts smooth textures that are agreeable to the mind. They love what they desire and long for it with greedy pursuit."

If a bhikṣu delights in and approves of the mind dwelling therein, and having become attached, he abides in it, he will then find pleasure in delusion; from this, he brings about affliction, sorrow, and distress.
Suppose, Bhadrika!
When one sees forms with the eyes, if one does not take delight in those things that are pleasing to the eye, and the mind does not dwell upon them, then affliction and distress will be eliminated.
The same applies to the ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind; this is a brief presentation of the essential Dharma.
The Buddha’s instruction is to admonish you as you now wish to travel.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, there is a country named Śroṇāparāntaka—which in the Jin language is called ‘What is Heard Desires Victory’—and I wish to travel to that country.”
The Buddha said:
“The people of that land are wicked and harbor coarse intentions; they are unable to be gentle and instead delight in inciting strife and disorder among others.
Suppose the malicious people of that land, with alienated hearts, were to revile and insult you—how would you respond?”
"Suppose that wicked people with hostile minds in that land should revile and insult me;
I shall think to myself: 'Even those who love and respect me still forgive me and do not push me with their hands.'"
The Buddha said,
"Even if they were to strike you,
what would you do? Pūrṇa replied:
"One should mindfully think:
'They still love me, respect me, and regard me as virtuous, good, gentle, and mild; they do not strike or throw tiles and stones at me.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Suppose someone were to strike you with tiles or stones; what would you do?
Pūrṇa replied, "The people of that country are virtuous, benevolent, harmonious, and refined; they will not injure or strike my body with blades or staves."
The Buddha said, "Suppose knives and staves were to wound and strike your body;
what would you do? Pūrṇa replied:
"I shall think to myself:
'The people of that country are kind, gentle, mild, and refined; they will not harm my body or life with sharp blades.
The Buddha said:
"Even if a sharp blade were to take your life, what would you do?
Pūrṇa replied: "I would think to myself:"

"The body possesses the six sense organs, which are its affliction; one grows weary of the body's manifold troubles and impurities that flow forth. Seeking a blade as food, the will is fixed solely upon flavor; entering into stillness, one takes the blade as food."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Pūrṇa!
You are capable of enduring such circumstances; being disciplined, tranquil, patient, and virtuous, you may dwell in that land according to your wishes."

Thereupon, Pūrṇa rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and went to his own quarters. That very night, he put away his bedding and lay down to sleep peacefully; then, at dawn, he dressed, took up his bowl, and set out for that kingdom.

Thereupon, while remaining in that country for one summer retreat, he taught and exhorted them to take up the practice, inviting five hundred laymen (*upāsaka*) and five hundred laywomen (*upāsikā*). He established five hundred monasteries, five hundred cave-dwellings, and five hundred sets of beds and benches, as well as five hundred each of Dharma seats, mats, robes, and pillows.
He transformed five hundred people, making them all śramaṇas; within that same year, they realized the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) and subsequently entered parinirvāṇa.

Not long after their parinirvāṇa, an incalculable multitude of thousands of bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and standing to one side, addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"There was a bhikṣu named Pūrṇa, for whom the Buddha briefly expounded the essential Dharma. Since he has already entered parinirvāṇa not long ago, what did he attain and what did he realize?"
The Buddha said: “O bhikṣus!

That son of good family has already aroused the three types of supernormal knowledge and attained the six higher powers. He observes the Dharma in accordance with truth, finding no equal to himself; he attends to no other matters but preaches only the scriptural teachings of the Dharma. His outflows are exhausted and he is free from all defilement; having transcended conceptual thought, he is liberated through wisdom.”

Now, having attained supreme mastery over all the supernormal powers regarding the Dharma and realized its perfection, he has severed the cycle of birth and death; he proclaims that the holy life has been lived and what was to be done has been accomplished. With the fundamental wisdom regarding name-and-form being rare and non-arising, he is fully endowed with noble knowledge and has attained the state of an Arhat.
At that time, there was no one who did not praise and extol the boundless Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
Thus spoke the Buddha;
the bhikṣus were all filled with joy.
The Sūtra on the Son of Full Fulfillment Spoken by the Buddha
